risk.headline: High exposure highest risk on this cluster

why.items.head: Offboarding does not revoke it
why.items.body: Removing someone from an LDAP group revokes their access everywhere at once. A binding that names the person keeps granting after they leave the team, change role, or leave the company — until somebody remembers it exists.

why.items.head: Invisible to access review
why.items.body: Every group-based review — including the rest of this dashboard — answers “who is in the group?”. These grants are attached to no group, so a clean review can coexist with standing access nobody approved.

why.items.head: No approval trail
why.items.body: Group membership is granted in the enterprise directory, with a request and an approver. A hand-made binding records only who ran oc, and only for as long as the audit log is retained.

exposure.note: Ranked by the worst privilege granted, not by count — one forgotten cluster-admin matters more than twenty view grants.
exposure.platform_note: 24 platform identities excluded — system components and kubeadmin are break-glass and cluster-internal, with nowhere to migrate to.
runbook: Identify the role. Match the grant to the LDAP group the operator already syncs for that privilege — the naming convention encodes it (<app>-ns-admin, -ns-developer, -ns-audit).
Add the person to that group in the enterprise directory, through the normal request-and-approve path. Access now has an owner and an audit trail.
Wait one sync and confirm on the Groups tab that they appear as a member. Do not skip this — deleting first leaves them locked out.
Delete the direct binding. oc delete rolebinding <name> -n <namespace>
Confirm it is gone here on the next refresh.
runbook.goal: Operational goal: zero rows on this page. At zero, one directory change offboards a person from the entire cluster, and an access review that reads clean is clean.
grants.note: The per-namespace table above is the view to work from. This is the flat detail list — collapsed by default on purpose, because on a cluster with thousands of direct grants rendering every row costs time nobody gets value from.

detail.cards: Who reaches it, and through which group · 0 · 1 platform
detail.notes: Carries none of the captured labels (company.net/mnemonic, company.net/app-environment, company.net/oud-group) — outside the naming convention, so no mnemonic-based report will ever pick it up.
The answer the triangle exists for: a namespace, back to the groups that grant it, back to the people in those groups.

Also reached cluster-wide, by 53 bindings that grant every namespace: app-ocp-rbac-alpha-cluster-admin (admin), app-ocp-rbac-demo-cluster-admin (admin), app-ocp-rbac-newteam-cluster-admin (admin), app-ocp-rbac-platform-cluster-admin (admin), app-ocp-rbac-test-cluster-admin (admin), app-ocp-rbac-alpha-database-admin (database-admin), app-ocp-rbac-alpha-cluster-developer (edit), app-ocp-rbac-demo-cluster-developer (edit), app-ocp-rbac-finance-cluster-developer (edit), app-ocp-rbac-platform-cluster-developer (edit), app-ocp-rbac-groupsync-ns-auditor (group-sync-dashboard-report-auditor), app-ocp-rbac-alpha-cluster-audit (view), app-ocp-rbac-demo-cluster-audit (view), dana.lee (cluster-reader, named directly), jdoe (edit, named directly), ocp-oauth-bind-serviceid (group-sync-dashboard-cluster-poller, named directly); and 37 platform bindings to 12 virtual groups (system:authenticated, system:nodes, system:authenticated:oauth, … 9 more) that every namespace carries.
A person named by a binding rather than reached through a group — the rows a directory change cannot offboard. The operational goal for this card is zero.
